This map shows our 2025 Early Voting locations. These locations are symbolized by how many people turned out to vote at each location. Orange represents our busiest polling sites with long lines, Green shows our least busy sites, and Yellow are sites with average turnout numbers. Some of our busiest sites are located near sites which were much less busy. Use this map to plan your next trip to the polls by visiting a green site as these often have short lines or no line at all.


This map also has a search function, so you can enter your address and see nearby polling locations.

This scene is an attempt to better illustrate voter density vs land area. The precinct symbology is identical to the election results maps on the main page. The z-axis is extruded vertically based on the number of registered voters per acre in each precinct. IE, precincts with a small number of registered voters over a large area are flat, and precincts with a very high number of voters in a small area are tall.


Use your mouse to navigate this scene: The scroll wheel zooms in and out, the left mouse button drags the entire scene, and the right mouse button rotates the scene. There's a Home button in the top left to reset.

This choropleth map is the result of a Moran’s I and LISA analysis conducted within R-Studio. Moran’s I and LISA (Local Indicators of Spatial Autocorrelation) are statistical tools that help to identify patterns in spatial data, such as neighborhoods where voters tend to mostly vote the same way. Spatial Autocorrelation refers to the tendency of similar values clustering together geographically.


Moran’s I analysis seeks to measure how clustered a set of variables are over the entire area. The values produced by a Moran’s I test indicates whether precincts with similar voting patterns are clustered together, randomly distributed, or evenly dispersed. In this analysis, a Moran’s I value of 0.25 indicates significant clustering of similar voters. In other words, people who live near each other tend to vote in similar ways.


LISA is a continuation of Moran’s I and pinpoints where these clusters occur. LISA searches for hotspots, which are groups of precincts with strong voter similarity. Hotspots are useful for identifying large areas of voters who demonstrate uniform support for one political party over another.


Combining these two analyses reveals the voting preferences of Bexar and highlights patterns of strong political alignment within our county.

Precincts with a low density of registered voters (voters per acre < 1) were not included in this analysis.  Retaining these precincts would skew the clusters as these precincts tend to have heavily uniform voting preferences and the results would be less meaningful otherwise.


The R-Studio script used to produce this analysis can be downloaded here along with the shapefile of the results.  Be sure to install the required libraries and update the file paths if trying to run this script.

If we take the Presidential election spatial autocorrelation maps from 2012 through 2024 and extract precinct clusters which are present on all of them, then we get a composite of clusters within Bexar. This composite map shows precincts whose voters have consistently supported one party over another and are adjacent to other precincts with similar voting patterns.


﻿These voters have held uniform voting habits over the last 12 years.


Precinct boundaries change over time, so the precincts represented here are from 2024.  A shapefile of this data is available for download.
